content: Disasters, particularly epidemics or outbreaks, amplify numerous ethical challenges in healthcare delivery, including issues of privacy, confidentiality, informed consent, community engagement, benefit sharing, and resource allocation. As of now, there are no approved treatments or prophylactic products proven to be both safe and effective for COVID-19, a situation reminiscent of previous outbreaks like Ebola virus disease, Zika virus disease, and Lassa fever. This underscores the critical need for research on new medications or vaccines during pandemics, necessitating that research ethics committees be prepared to conduct rapid reviews of related research projects. Countries vary in their readiness to provide ethical reviews for epidemic-related research. Regardless of prior preparatory efforts, ethics committees must take specific actions to prepare for the rapid review of emergency research protocols, such as those for COVID-19. Following the 2014 Ebola outbreak, numerous articles and reports addressed ethical issues in outbreak research and research ethics governance. Key concerns included the time sensitivity of reviews and the balance between ensuring quality and timeliness while protecting clinical trial participants, many of whom are in urgent need of life-saving interventions. Two workshops in 2018 focused on these issues. The first, titled Ethics preparedness: facilitating ethics review during outbreaks, was organized by ALERRT (African Coalition for Epidemic Research, Response, and Training) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in Dakar, Senegal. The second, Ethics review of research on Lassa and other infectious disease outbreaks, was organized by WHO in Abuja, Nigeria. These workshops provided recommendations for national and institutional research ethics committees to adapt their standard operating procedures to respond efficiently during pandemics. Once an outbreak is declared an emergency by the public health authority of a country, several processes—such as drafting documents, translations, and approvals—must occur simultaneously rather than sequentially to expedite the commencement of research. The contributions of research ethics committee members are highly valued, especially as they may also be managing other responsibilities or dealing with personal challenges during public health emergencies. To mitigate risks associated with face-to-face meetings during epidemics or pandemics, virtual meetings and review processes should be considered whenever feasible. When a protocol is submitted in a language different from that of the review, key documents such as the synopsis, plan, consent or assent forms, and data collection tools should be submitted in the official language of the reviewing country. Other documents should follow as soon as possible. To facilitate rapid, time-sensitive reviews, research ethics committees should consider the following recommendations for modifying their standard operating procedures: 1. Include a checklist in the ethics review form to identify the research as outbreak-related, describe prior research data on the disease, and ensure the inclusion of local investigators with relevant qualifications and experience. 2. Require additional documents, such as collaboration letters with sponsors and funders, monitoring and safety management plans, data-sharing agreements, and dissemination procedures for findings. 3. Establish a process for rapid review, communicating this to researchers and addressing potential delays for non-emergency research. 4. Identify surge capacity for reviews, set up systems for remote discussions, and ensure access to necessary technology. 5. Pre-identify committee members with specialized training or experience in outbreak-related research to handle the review workload efficiently. 6. Alert committee members about imminent or ongoing outbreaks to confirm their availability for rapid reviews. 7. Identify subject matter experts and ethics specialists willing to serve as ad hoc members during outbreaks. 8. Define a quorum as one-third of the committee members, including pre-identified relevant individuals. 9. Allow pre-identified members who submit their reviews but cannot attend meetings to count toward the quorum. 10. Circulate revised standard operating procedures to all committee members. 11. Conduct review meetings virtually or electronically, especially during highly infectious outbreaks like COVID-19. 12. Accept electronic protocol submissions to save time, with hard copies submitted later if required. 13. Avoid mandatory face-to-face meetings with principal investigators, opting for virtual venues if necessary. 14. Send protocols to reviewers within 24 hours of submission. 15. Require reviewers to complete their reviews within a specified timeframe, typically three days during an outbreak. 16. Communicate consolidated reviews and suggestions (or approvals) to principal investigators within five days. 17. Use electronic or telephonic communication to seek clarifications from principal investigators, saving time. 18. Require principal investigators to respond to reviews within 48 hours. 19. Identify focal points for communication within national and institutional ethics committees early in the process. 20. Document and archive all communications. These measures aim to ensure that research ethics committees can respond effectively and ethically during public health emergencies, balancing the urgency of research with the protection of participants and the integrity of the review process.
